title: Hosted API demo - chat & text generation basics
summary: Intro + hosted API walkthrough focusing on chat/text generation: streaming, request params, retries and basic security questions. Good fit for rapid prototyping; customer concerned about latency, cost and data residency. Agreed next steps: send pricing, security pack, and run a short benchmark with their prompt set.
transcript:
00:00 Jordan Miles: Hey everybody, I'm Jordan from Redwood, thanks for joining. Quick intro, Priya is our solutions engineer who will walk through the runtime and demo, and I'll handle pricing and next steps.
00:18 Ethan Cole: Hey thanks, Jordan, we appreciate it. Timebox is 45 minutes, we want to understand hosted capabilities, streaming, and how retries work, because we have a customer-facing chat assistant.
00:33 Jordan Miles: Awesome, that's right in our sweet spot. Priya, over to you.
00:38 Priya Nair: Great thanks. So I'll share my screen, ok? Can everyone see the Redwood console? (slight pause) Cool. So high level, hosted API gives you text, chat, embeddings, rerank. Today we'll focus on chat/text generation basics — streaming, params, and retries.
01:05 Maya Lin: Quick question while you start — do you have a region in us-west or EU for residency?
01:13 Priya Nair: Yes, hosted has regional endpoints, us-west and eu-west, and we can restrict data to those regions. For strict residency you may want Private, but many customers use hosted with region pinning.
01:27 Jordan Miles: Also we have configurable retention and enterprise contracts for longer retention and SOC2 requirements.
01:35 Priya Nair: Ok demo, simple chat request: message history, system prompt, user prompt. We send to /v1/chat/completions, you can enable streaming via SSE, chunked responses, so tokens arrive as they are generated. I'll send a sample prompt — "Summarize this transaction for compliance" — and enable streaming.
01:55 (demo noise)
02:06 Priya Nair: You can see tokens coming in, there may be small reordering artifacts — that's normal — the client reconstructs final text. Streaming reduces time-to-first-byte which helps user perceived latency for chat.
02:28 Ethan Cole: What's typical end-to-end latency for a single-turn 120 token response?
02:35 Priya Nair: On hosted, median p95 depends on model and seq length. For our curated Llama-2/Redwood variants at 120 tokens we often see 200-400ms to first token and 600-900ms to finish in our us-west region; your mileage will vary, esp if you add heavy system instructions.
03:02 Maya Lin: And cost per token?
03:05 Jordan Miles: Pricing depends on model class, but we bill per input/output tokens; I'll follow up with a pricing sheet. We also recommend batching/kv cache for chat sessions to reduce cost.
03:18 Priya Nair: Back to params — temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stop sequences, presence/ frequency penalties. For deterministic outputs we set temperature to 0 or 0.1. For creative summarization 0.7.
03:38 Priya Nair: Also show you "max_output_tokens" vs server-side safety truncation. If you set stop sequences, streaming will end when stop is observed and the client gets final event.
03:52 Sara Ortiz: How do retries interact with streaming? If a stream fails in the middle, do we re-request and double-charge?
03:59 Priya Nair: Good question. We recommend idempotency keys on requests. For non-streamed calls retry is simple — server returns final tokens and you get billed once. For streaming, if the connection drops, you can re-establish with the same idempotency key; our runtime will detect partial completion and either resume or tell you to retry from start. Billing is handled to avoid double-charge where possible but depends on how the client reconnects.
04:30 Ethan Cole: Is there a client SDK that handles reconnection/resume?
04:35 Priya Nair: We provide SDKs for Node/Python with helpers for SSE streams and simple retry logic. For complex resume semantics you can use conversation-level caching (KV cache) to avoid re-synthesizing earlier tokens.
04:50 Jordan Miles: We also have server-side continuous batching which groups small requests to improve throughput — this affects latency/cost tradeoffs. We'll share a best-practices doc.
05:05 Maya Lin: About concurrency — we may have spikes of 200 QPS. Can hosted handle that or would we need Dedicated?
05:12 Priya Nair: Hosted can handle bursts but for sustained high QPS, Dedicated/reserved capacity is recommended. Hosted is multitenant and does autoscaling, but latency SLOs at very high sustained throughput are better on Dedicated.
05:30 (demo continues)
06:02 Priya Nair: Now show request examples — you'll see a JSON body with messages array and parameters. Notice we include a "request_id" and optional "idempotency_token".
06:20 Maya Lin: On the JSON, where do we pass metadata for our routing? Like customer_id?
06:25 Priya Nair: You can send metadata headers for logging/labels; we have per-request routing policies. For privacy don't send PII in metadata.
06:36 Ethan Cole: Security — SSO, audit logs, KMS?
06:40 Jordan Miles: We support SAML/SSO, fine-grained RBAC in the console, audit logs with export, and enterprise KMS integrations for Private. For hosted, encryption at rest with provider-managed keys by default; customer-managed KMS is available on Dedicated/Private.
07:05 Maya Lin: Do you have SOC2 and pen test reports?
07:10 Jordan Miles: Yes, will send SOC2 attestation and a redacted penetration test summary in the security pack.
07:18 (noise)
07:25 Priya Nair: Quick talk about model choices — generation quality vs cost. We surface model profiles; you can choose smaller quantized variants for cheaper throughput, or larger models for better coherence.
07:40 Ethan Cole: We currently use OpenAI for prototyping. What are common migration issues?
07:48 Priya Nair: Prompt differences, tokenization nuances, temperature defaults. Also sometimes hallucination behavior differs. We provide a migration checklist and prompt tuning examples; we can run a quick side-by-side benchmark with your prompts.
08:06 Jordan Miles: Competitors you might evaluate include OpenAI, Anthropic, and cloud providers like Bedrock. We try to compete on cost predictability and production-grade runtime.
08:22 Maya Lin: Ok, demo of streaming SDK — Priya shows Node snippet with event handlers for "data" and "end".
08:35 Priya Nair: Note we surface partial tokens and also an "is_final" event. Clients can render partial text to give immediate feedback then finalize when stream ends.
09:00 Ethan Cole: What about rate limits and quotas?
09:04 Jordan Miles: Hosted per-account quotas, rate limits per token/sec and rps. For higher needs we set custom limits.
09:12 Maya Lin: Error modes — transient server errors vs model internal errors?
09:16 Priya Nair: 5xx transient — retry with backoff and idempotency. 4xx client errors mean fix prompt or params. For model safety interventions we return a structured error you can handle.
09:35 Ethan Cole: Can we do streaming plus function/tool calling?
09:39 Priya Nair: Yes, we support streaming with tool calls. Tools output is emitted as structured events you can parse; client SDKs help wire that up.
10:02 (demo pause)
10:10 Priya Nair: Quick notes on batching and KV caching: for chat we cache embeddings or KV keys so model doesn't re-encode long history. This reduces tokens and cost.
10:30 Maya Lin: For our compliance flow we need deterministic summaries, and we need to re-run with same prompt and get same output. Any recommendations?
10:38 Priya Nair: Set temperature to 0, fix stop tokens, and pin model version. Also capture model sha/version from response metadata. We'll show how to pin.
11:00 Jordan Miles: Ok moving to reliability — we'll do retries for timeouts, use idempotency tokens, and instrument request IDs from logs. Priya will share trace snippets you can add to your observability.
11:20 (customer asks about PII)
11:25 Sara Ortiz: If a user posts SSNs by accident, what are your retention/removal tools?
11:30 Jordan Miles: For hosted we have redaction hooks and opt-out ingestion; enterprise customers get additional controls and audit logs. We'll include the data handling section in the security pack.
11:48 Priya Nair: End-to-end demo final: show a chat flow with streaming, a retry simulation where we intentionally drop connection and then reconnect with same idempotency token — runtime reports partial and resumes or returns completed output.
12:15 Ethan Cole: That resume behavior is helpful. We'll want to try with our real prompts.
12:22 Jordan Miles: Great. Time for Q&A and next steps?
12:27 Maya Lin: Timeline: we want an evaluation in the next 2 weeks, pilot for 4-6 weeks. Main success criteria: latency under 1s for first token p95, cost per active session < $0.02, reproducible summaries.
12:45 Jordan Miles: Good. Priya will run a benchmark, I'll send pricing and security docs.
12:52 (wrap)
13:00 Jordan Miles: Recap — share pricing, SOC2/pen test, SDK snippets, and run benchmark with your prompt set. Next call to review results.
13:12 Ethan Cole: Thanks everyone, we'll send prompt set and sample traffic patterns by EOD tomorrow.
13:20 Jordan Miles: Perfect, talk soon!
